claim: The CRISPR/Cas9 system is a robust genome editing technology that works in human cells, animals and plants based on the RNA-programmed DNA cleaving activity of the Cas9 enzyme.
source: The CRISPR/Cas9 system is a robust genome editing technology that works in human cells, animals and plants based on the RNA-programmed DNA cleaving activity of the Cas9 enzyme.
evidence: This is a general statement about CRISPR/Cas9 technology that draws from established scientific knowledge and consensus in the field.

claim: New genetic information can be introduced site-specifically and with high efficiency by homology-directed repair (HDR) of Cas9-induced site-specific double-strand DNA breaks using timed delivery of Cas9-guide RNA ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes.
source: Building on previous work (Jinek et al., 2013), we show here that new genetic information can be introduced site-specifically and with high efficiency by homology-directed repair (HDR) of Cas9-induced site-specific double-strand DNA breaks using timed delivery of Cas9-guide RNA ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and builds on cited previous work.

claim: Cas9 RNP-mediated HDR in HEK293T, human primary neonatal fibroblast and human embryonic stem cells was increased dramatically relative to experiments in unsynchronized cells.
source: Cas9 RNP-mediated HDR in HEK293T, human primary neonatal fibroblast and human embryonic stem cells was increased dramatically relative to experiments in unsynchronized cells, with rates of HDR up to 38% observed in HEK293T cells.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing HDR rates in different cell types.

claim: Rates of HDR up to 38% were observed in HEK293T cells using timed delivery of Cas9 RNPs.
source: Cas9 RNP-mediated HDR in HEK293T, human primary neonatal fibroblast and human embryonic stem cells was increased dramatically relative to experiments in unsynchronized cells, with rates of HDR up to 38% observed in HEK293T cells.
evidence: This specific quantitative result is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: Sequencing of on- and potential off-target sites showed that editing occurred with high fidelity.
source: Sequencing of on- and potential off-target sites showed that editing occurred with high fidelity, while cell mortality was minimized.
evidence: This claim is supported by deep sequencing data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cell mortality was minimized using the timed delivery approach.
source: Sequencing of on- and potential off-target sites showed that editing occurred with high fidelity, while cell mortality was minimized.
evidence: This is supported by observations of cell viability and morphology described in the manuscript.

claim: The approach provides a simple and highly effective strategy for enhancing site-specific genome engineering in both transformed and primary human cells.
source: This approach provides a simple and highly effective strategy for enhancing site-specific genome engineering in both transformed and primary human cells.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental results showing enhanced HDR in multiple cell types.

claim: Cas9 enables site-specific genome engineering by introducing double-strand breaks (DSB) at guide RNA-specified chromosomal loci of interest.
source: The CRISPR-associated enzyme Cas9 enables site-specific genome engineering by introducing double-strand breaks (DSB) at guide RNA-specified chromosomal loci of interest (Cong et al., 2013; Jinek et al., 2013; Mali et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cells repair DSBs using the non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) or homology-directed repair (HDR) pathways.
source: Cells repair DSBs using the non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) or homology-directed repair (HDR) pathways.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about DNA repair mechanisms.

claim: The NHEJ pathway generates variable insertions or deletions (indels) at the DSB.
source: The NHEJ pathway generates variable insertions or deletions (indels) at the DSB, while HDR employs homologous donor DNA sequences from sister chromatids, homologous chromosomes or exogenous DNA molecules to produce precise insertions, deletions or base substitutions at a DSB site or between two DSBs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the NHEJ DNA repair pathway.

claim: HDR employs homologous donor DNA sequences from sister chromatids, homologous chromosomes or exogenous DNA molecules to produce precise insertions, deletions or base substitutions at a DSB site or between two DSBs.
source: The NHEJ pathway generates variable insertions or deletions (indels) at the DSB, while HDR employs homologous donor DNA sequences from sister chromatids, homologous chromosomes or exogenous DNA molecules to produce precise insertions, deletions or base substitutions at a DSB site or between two DSBs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the HDR DNA repair pathway.

claim: The phase of the cell cycle largely governs the choice of DNA repair pathway between NHEJ and HDR.
source: Although cells have differing abilities to repair DSBs using NHEJ or HDR, the phase of the cell cycle largely governs the choice of pathway.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cell cycle regulation of DNA repair pathways.

claim: NHEJ dominates DNA repair during G1, S and G2 phases.
source: NHEJ dominates DNA repair during G1, S and G2 phases, whereas HDR is restricted to late S and G2 phases when DNA replication is completed and sister chromatids are available to serve as repair templates (Heyer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: HDR is restricted to late S and G2 phases when DNA replication is completed and sister chromatids are available to serve as repair templates.
source: NHEJ dominates DNA repair during G1, S and G2 phases, whereas HDR is restricted to late S and G2 phases when DNA replication is completed and sister chromatids are available to serve as repair templates (Heyer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: HDR is specifically down-regulated at M phase and early G1 to prevent telomere fusion.
source: Impediments to HDR include competition with NHEJ in S and G2 phases and specific down-regulation of HDR at M phase and early G1 to prevent telomere fusion (Orthwein et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Chemical or genetic interruption of the NHEJ pathway can favor HDR.
source: Although chemical or genetic interruption of the NHEJ pathway can favor HDR (Shrivastav et al., 2008), such manipulations can be difficult to employ, harmful to cells or both.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Chemical or genetic interruption of the NHEJ pathway can be difficult to employ, harmful to cells or both.
source: Although chemical or genetic interruption of the NHEJ pathway can favor HDR (Shrivastav et al., 2008), such manipulations can be difficult to employ, harmful to cells or both.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited work and general knowledge.

claim: High cleavage activity of programmable nucleases does not necessarily correlate with efficient HDR-induced genome editing.
source: Consequently, high cleavage activity of programmable nucleases does not necessarily correlate with efficient HDR-induced genome editing.
evidence: This is inferred from the discussion of NHEJ/HDR competition and pathway choice.

claim: The strategy combines well-established cell cycle synchronization techniques with direct nucleofection of pre-assembled Cas9 ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes to achieve controlled nuclease action at the phase of the cell cycle best for HDR.
source: This strategy combines well-established cell cycle synchronization techniques with direct nucleofection of pre-assembled Cas9 ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes to achieve controlled nuclease action at the phase of the cell cycle best for HDR (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach shown in Figure 1A.

claim: HEK293T, human primary neonatal fibroblast and H9 human embryonic stem cells demonstrated robust HDR-mediated genome editing at levels up to 38% with no detected off-target editing.
source: HEK293T, human primary neonatal fibroblast and H9 human embryonic stem cells demonstrated robust HDR-mediated genome editing at levels up to 38% with no detected off-target editing.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data including deep sequencing analysis.

claim: The approach enables efficient mutation, repair and tagging of endogenous loci in a rapid and predictable manner.
source: These results establish a superior approach to Cas9-mediated human genome engineering that enables efficient mutation, repair and tagging of endogenous loci in a rapid and predictable manner.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results demonstrating high HDR efficiency.

claim: Lovastatin blocks cells at early G1 and partially at G2/M phase.
source: Chemical inhibitors used to arrest cells at specific phases of cell cycle included lovastatin (Lov), which blocks at early G1 and partially at G2/M phase; mimosine (Mim), aphidicolin (Aph), thymidine (Thy) and hydroxyurea (HU) which arrest cells at the G1-S border prior to onset of DNA replication; and nocodazole (Noc) which causes arrest at G2/M phase.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about cell cycle inhibitors and confirmed by FACS analysis shown in the manuscript.

claim: Mimosine, aphidicolin, thymidine and hydroxyurea arrest cells at the G1-S border prior to onset of DNA replication.
source: Chemical inhibitors used to arrest cells at specific phases of cell cycle included lovastatin (Lov), which blocks at early G1 and partially at G2/M phase; mimosine (Mim), aphidicolin (Aph), thymidine (Thy) and hydroxyurea (HU) which arrest cells at the G1-S border prior to onset of DNA replication; and nocodazole (Noc) which causes arrest at G2/M phase.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about cell cycle inhibitors and confirmed by FACS analysis shown in the manuscript.

claim: Nocodazole causes arrest at G2/M phase.
source: Chemical inhibitors used to arrest cells at specific phases of cell cycle included lovastatin (Lov), which blocks at early G1 and partially at G2/M phase; mimosine (Mim), aphidicolin (Aph), thymidine (Thy) and hydroxyurea (HU) which arrest cells at the G1-S border prior to onset of DNA replication; and nocodazole (Noc) which causes arrest at G2/M phase.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about cell cycle inhibitors and confirmed by FACS analysis shown in the manuscript.

claim: Both aphidicolin and nocodazole led to pronounced increases in Cas9-mediated editing frequencies.
source: After 24 hr, cells were analyzed for HDR (specifically, exogenous donor template mediated HDR) or total editing (TE, defined as the sum of all NHEJ and HDR events that give rise to indels) at the Cas9 cleavage site within EMX1, showing that both aphidicolin and nocodazole led to pronounced increases in Cas9-mediated editing frequencies (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: The enhancement in editing is more evident at lower Cas9 RNP concentration (30 ρmol).
source: The enhancement is more evident at lower Cas9 RNP concentration (30 ρmol), improving HDR rates from ∼9% in unsynchronized cells to ∼14% with aphidicolin and ∼20% with nocodazole (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Aphidicolin improved HDR rates from ∼9% in unsynchronized cells to ∼14% at 30 ρmol Cas9 RNP.
source: The enhancement is more evident at lower Cas9 RNP concentration (30 ρmol), improving HDR rates from ∼9% in unsynchronized cells to ∼14% with aphidicolin and ∼20% with nocodazole (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Nocodazole improved HDR rates from ∼9% in unsynchronized cells to ∼20% at 30 ρmol Cas9 RNP.
source: The enhancement is more evident at lower Cas9 RNP concentration (30 ρmol), improving HDR rates from ∼9% in unsynchronized cells to ∼14% with aphidicolin and ∼20% with nocodazole (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The highest HDR frequency achieved was 31% with nocodazole synchronization and 100 ρmol of Cas9 RNP.
source: The highest HDR frequency achieved was 31% with nocodazole synchronization and 100 ρmol of Cas9 RNP.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: 1 day after nocodazole release the synchronized cells were cycling like unsynchronized controls and appeared morphologically normal.
source: Importantly, 1 day after nocodazole release the synchronized cells were cycling like unsynchronized controls and appeared morphologically normal (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis and microscopy shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The overall frequencies of TE and HDR increased proportionally with increasing Cas9 RNP concentration.
source: The overall frequencies of TE and HDR increased proportionally with increasing Cas9 RNP concentration (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Synchronization increased the TE frequency twofold at 10 ρmol and 1.5-fold at 30 ρmol Cas9 RNP.
source: Synchronization increased the TE frequency twofold at 10 ρmol and 1.5-fold at 30 ρmol Cas9 RNP, but the enhancement diminished at 100 ρmol.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The enhancement in TE frequency diminished at 100 ρmol Cas9 RNP.
source: Synchronization increased the TE frequency twofold at 10 ρmol and 1.5-fold at 30 ρmol Cas9 RNP, but the enhancement diminished at 100 ρmol.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The HDR frequency increased dramatically with synchronization, especially at lower concentrations of Cas9 RNP, from undetectable to 9–15% at 10 ρmol of Cas9 RNP.
source: The HDR frequency also increased dramatically with synchronization, especially at lower concentrations of Cas9 RNP, from undetectable to 9–15% at 10 ρmol of Cas9 RNP, and from 6–12% to 22–28% at 30 ρmol (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The HDR frequency increased from 6–12% to 22–28% at 30 ρmol Cas9 RNP with synchronization.
source: The HDR frequency also increased dramatically with synchronization, especially at lower concentrations of Cas9 RNP, from undetectable to 9–15% at 10 ρmol of Cas9 RNP, and from 6–12% to 22–28% at 30 ρmol (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Timed delivery of Cas9 RNP into M-phase synchronized HEK293T cells enhances HDR by several fold above the levels observed without synchronization.
source: These results demonstrate that timed delivery of Cas9 RNP into M-phase synchronized HEK293T cells enhances HDR by several fold above the levels observed without synchronization.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing increased HDR with nocodazole synchronization.

claim: Both (+) and (−) strand orientations of ssODNA HDR templates yielded comparable levels of HDR at the DYRK1 locus.
source: We assayed two ssODNA HDR templates spanning the same sequence but with different orientations: one identical to the target strand sequence (+strand) and the other its complement (−strand) (Figure 2B). Both of these templates yielded comparable levels of HDR.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Nocodazole synchronization enhanced the TE frequencies more than twofold at all doses of Cas9 RNP at the DYRK1 locus.
source: Strikingly, nocodazole synchronization enhanced the TE frequencies more than twofold and HDR frequencies over sixfold at all doses of Cas9 RNP (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Nocodazole synchronization enhanced HDR frequencies over sixfold at all doses of Cas9 RNP at the DYRK1 locus.
source: Strikingly, nocodazole synchronization enhanced the TE frequencies more than twofold and HDR frequencies over sixfold at all doses of Cas9 RNP (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Nocodazole synchronization reduced the requirement for high Cas9 RNP concentrations, producing 5–6% HDR at 10 ρmol of Cas9 at the DYRK1 locus.
source: Moreover, nocodazole synchronization reduced the requirement for high Cas9 RNP concentrations, producing 5–6% HDR at 10 ρmol of Cas9; 10-fold more Cas9 RNP was required to achieve the same HDR frequency in unsynchronized cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 10-fold more Cas9 RNP was required to achieve the same HDR frequency in unsynchronized cells compared to nocodazole synchronized cells at the DYRK1 locus.
source: Moreover, nocodazole synchronization reduced the requirement for high Cas9 RNP concentrations, producing 5–6% HDR at 10 ρmol of Cas9; 10-fold more Cas9 RNP was required to achieve the same HDR frequency in unsynchronized cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data comparing synchronized and unsynchronized conditions.

claim: CXCR4 is a chemokine receptor implicated in HIV entry.
source: We also programmed Cas9 RNPs to target the CXCR4 gene, a chemokine receptor implicated in HIV entry (Feng et al., 1996) and cancer metastasis (Murphy, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: CXCR4 is implicated in cancer metastasis.
source: We also programmed Cas9 RNPs to target the CXCR4 gene, a chemokine receptor implicated in HIV entry (Feng et al., 1996) and cancer metastasis (Murphy, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The enhancement in TE and HDR frequencies at CXCR4 was comparable to those observed for the DYRK1 target site.
source: The enhancement in TE and HDR frequencies at CXCR4 was comparable to those observed for the DYRK1 target site (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Nocodazole synchronization yielded 27% HDR at 10 ρmol of Cas9 RNP at the CXCR4 locus.
source: In this case, nocodazole synchronization yielded 27% HDR at 10 ρmol of Cas9 RNP.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A comparable level of HDR in the unsynchronized cells would require 100 ρmol of RNP at the CXCR4 locus.
source: A comparable level of HDR in the unsynchronized cells would require 100 ρmol of RNP.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data comparing synchronized and unsynchronized conditions.

claim: Nocodazole synchronization is a highly effective and broadly applicable method to enhance the TE and HDR frequencies in HEK293T cells.
source: Collectively, the results from EMX1, DYRK1 and CXCR4 loci demonstrate that nocodazole synchronization is a highly effective and broadly applicable method to enhance the TE and HDR frequencies in HEK293T cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data at multiple loci.

claim: Off-target editing increases with increasing nucleic acid-based delivery of Cas9.
source: Off-target editing increases with increasing nucleic acid-based delivery of Cas9 (Fu et al., 2013; Hsu et al., 2013; Pattanayak et al., 2013; Mali et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cas9 RNP is short-lived.
source: We reasoned that the short-lived Cas9 RNP (Kim et al., 2014) and timed delivery would minimize off-target editing and that potential toxicity might be minimized by using lower RNP amounts.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: No off-target editing was detected above background levels under all conditions tested.
source: Importantly, no off-target editing was detected above background levels under all conditions, and increasing RNP dosage had no effect on off-target editing.
evidence: This is supported by deep sequencing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Increasing RNP dosage had no effect on off-target editing.
source: Importantly, no off-target editing was detected above background levels under all conditions, and increasing RNP dosage had no effect on off-target editing.
evidence: This is supported by deep sequencing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The TE and HDR frequencies detected by deep sequencing were comparable to gel densitometry results.
source: Overall, the TE and HDR frequencies detected by deep sequencing were comparable to our previous gel densitometry results (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of deep sequencing data with gel-based assays.

claim: There was no detectable HDR at the off-target loci.
source: Most importantly, there was no detectable HDR at the off-target loci.
evidence: This is supported by deep sequencing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Nocodazole synchronization increased the HDR/TE ratio by twofold at the EMX1 locus.
source: Although nocodazole synchronization increased the HDR/TE ratio by twofold at the EMX1 locus and fivefold at the DYRK1 locus, this ratio reached a maximum value of ∼33% across all RNP doses, suggesting that the maximum capacity of the HDR machinery in HEK293T cells is to repair ∼33% of DSBs.
evidence: This is supported by deep sequencing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Nocodazole synchronization increased the HDR/TE ratio by fivefold at the DYRK1 locus.
source: Although nocodazole synchronization increased the HDR/TE ratio by twofold at the EMX1 locus and fivefold at the DYRK1 locus, this ratio reached a maximum value of ∼33% across all RNP doses, suggesting that the maximum capacity of the HDR machinery in HEK293T cells is to repair ∼33% of DSBs.
evidence: This is supported by deep sequencing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The HDR/TE ratio reached a maximum value of ∼33% across all RNP doses.
source: Although nocodazole synchronization increased the HDR/TE ratio by twofold at the EMX1 locus and fivefold at the DYRK1 locus, this ratio reached a maximum value of ∼33% across all RNP doses, suggesting that the maximum capacity of the HDR machinery in HEK293T cells is to repair ∼33% of DSBs.
evidence: This is supported by deep sequencing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The maximum capacity of the HDR machinery in HEK293T cells is to repair ∼33% of DSBs.
source: Although nocodazole synchronization increased the HDR/TE ratio by twofold at the EMX1 locus and fivefold at the DYRK1 locus, this ratio reached a maximum value of ∼33% across all RNP doses, suggesting that the maximum capacity of the HDR machinery in HEK293T cells is to repair ∼33% of DSBs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the HDR/TE ratio plateaus at ~33%.

claim: Nocodazole synchronization produced higher HDR frequencies than observed in the unsynchronized cells.
source: As observed previously, nocodazole synchronization produced higher HDR frequencies than observed in the unsynchronized cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The aphidicolin block significantly reduced the HDR frequency.
source: As expected, the aphidicolin block significantly reduced the HDR frequency, supporting the conclusion that cells need to proceed through S phase, and possibly G2 as well, for highly efficient HDR.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Cells need to proceed through S phase, and possibly G2 as well, for highly efficient HDR.
source: As expected, the aphidicolin block significantly reduced the HDR frequency, supporting the conclusion that cells need to proceed through S phase, and possibly G2 as well, for highly efficient HDR.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that blocking S phase entry reduces HDR.

claim: DNA molecules with at least 60 nt of sequence homology flanking the Cas9 cleavage site were sufficient for highly efficient HDR of ∼19%.
source: DNA molecules with at least 60 nt of sequence homology flanking the Cas9 cleavage site were sufficient for highly efficient HDR of ∼19% (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Further extension of the homology arms to 90 nt increased the HDR frequency only slightly (∼20–23%).
source: Further extension of the homology arms to 90 nt increased the HDR frequency only slightly (∼20–23%).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Both (+) and (−) template orientations were similarly effective.
source: Both (+) and (−) template orientations were similarly effective, as also observed in the DYRK1 experiment.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: When double-stranded templates 6 and 7 were used, HDR frequencies were reduced to 7%.
source: When double-stranded templates 6 and 7 were used, HDR frequencies were reduced to 7%.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Double-stranded templates produced unusual banding patterns in the HindIII HDR assay implying the presence of a concatemerized HDR template or non-specific recombination products.
source: Moreover, unusual banding patterns in the HindIII HDR assay (Figure 3B) implied the presence of a concatemerized HDR template or non-specific recombination products, at least with short sequences as employed here.
evidence: This is inferred from the unusual banding patterns observed in the gel.

claim: Human primary neonatal fibroblasts and H9 human embryonic stem cells are challenging to transfect and typically show low levels of homologous recombination.
source: To expand our findings on the cell cycle synchronization method to other cell types, we targeted the EMX1 gene in human primary neonatal fibroblasts (neoFB) and H9 human embryonic stem (hES) cells. These cell types are challenging to transfect and typically show low levels of homologous recombination.
evidence: This is established knowledge about these cell types.

claim: In neoFB cells, enhancement in TE and HDR frequencies was observed with aphidicolin and thymidine treatments, which synchronize the cells at S phase.
source: In contrast to HEK293T cells, enhancement in TE and HDR frequencies was observed with aphidicolin and thymidine treatments, which synchronize the cells at S phase (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The TE frequencies in neoFB cells were 17% and 13% with aphidicolin and thymidine respectively, as opposed to 5% in the unsynchronized condition.
source: The TE frequencies were 17% and 13% with aphidicolin and thymidine respectively, as opposed to 5% in the unsynchronized condition.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: HDR frequency was very low across all conditions in neoFB cells and was not detected in the unsynchronized cells.
source: However, HDR frequency was very low across all conditions and was not detected in the unsynchronized cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: With aphidicolin synchronization, 0.6% and 1.3% HDR were detected at 30 and 100 ρmol Cas9 RNP respectively in neoFB cells.
source: With aphidicolin synchronization, 0.6% and 1.3% HDR were detected at 30 and 100 ρmol Cas9 RNP respectively.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Previous reports have shown ∼20% NHEJ with transfection of Cas9 RNPs in hES cells but didn't analyze HDR rates.
source: Previous reports have shown ∼20% NHEJ with transfection of Cas9 RNPs but didn't analyze HDR rates (Kim et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: HDR frequencies are low with nucleic acid-based delivery of Cas9 in hES cells.
source: Also, HDR frequencies are low with nucleic acid-based delivery of Cas9 (Hsu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Only nocodazole synchronization enhanced TE frequencies in hES cells to 9% at 30 ρmol and 28–31% at 100 ρmol Cas9 RNP.
source: Screening of chemical inhibitors showed that only nocodazole synchronization enhanced TE frequencies in hES cells to 9% at 30 ρmol and 28–31% at 100 ρmol Cas9 RNP; however, we did not detect HDR with the HDR template (−) sense strand (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: HDR was not detected with the HDR template (−) sense strand in hES cells with nocodazole synchronization alone.
source: Screening of chemical inhibitors showed that only nocodazole synchronization enhanced TE frequencies in hES cells to 9% at 30 ρmol and 28–31% at 100 ρmol Cas9 RNP; however, we did not detect HDR with the HDR template (−) sense strand (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Using nocodazole-aphidicolin sequential synchronization, ∼2% of HDR was detected at 100 ρmol Cas9 RNP in hES cells.
source: Using this approach, we detected ∼2% of HDR at 100 ρmol Cas9 RNP (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 3 days after release from cell cycle synchronization the hES cell cycle behavior was indistinguishable from unsynchronized control cultures, with no apparent changes in colony morphology.
source: 3 days after release from cell cycle synchronization the hES cell cycle behavior was indistinguishable from unsynchronized control cultures, with no apparent changes in colony morphology (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C); all colonies expressed high levels of alkaline phosphatase, a marker for pluripotency (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis and microscopy shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: All hES colonies expressed high levels of alkaline phosphatase, a marker for pluripotency, after cell cycle synchronization.
source: 3 days after release from cell cycle synchronization the hES cell cycle behavior was indistinguishable from unsynchronized control cultures, with no apparent changes in colony morphology (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C); all colonies expressed high levels of alkaline phosphatase, a marker for pluripotency (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by alkaline phosphatase staining shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: ROCK apoptosis inhibitor (10 μM) was required for survival of synchronized H9 ESCs after release when cultured at low density but not when cultured at high density.
source: ROCK apoptosis inhibitor (10 μM) was required for survival of synchronized H9 ESCs after release when cultured at low density but not when cultured at high density.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations described in the manuscript.

claim: Different cell types will have distinct requirements for synchronization to enhance Cas9 RNP-induced DNA repair.
source: These results suggest that different cell types will have distinct requirements for synchronization to enhance Cas9 RNP-induced DNA repair.
evidence: This is inferred from the different optimal synchronization conditions observed for HEK293T, neoFB, and hES cells.

claim: It may be possible to find conditions that will enable even higher levels of HDR in neoFB and hES cells using Cas9 RNP delivery.
source: Also, it may be possible to find conditions that will enable even higher levels of HDR in neoFB and hES cells using Cas9 RNP delivery.
evidence: This is speculation based on the results obtained.

claim: The approach has no detectable off-target editing.
source: Advantages of this approach include no detectable off-target editing, timed introduction of pre-assembled editing complexes into cells and simultaneous transfection of multiple Cas9 RNPs and donor DNAs.
evidence: This is supported by deep sequencing data showing no off-target editing.

claim: The approach allows timed introduction of pre-assembled editing complexes into cells.
source: Advantages of this approach include no detectable off-target editing, timed introduction of pre-assembled editing complexes into cells and simultaneous transfection of multiple Cas9 RNPs and donor DNAs.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach used.

claim: The approach allows simultaneous transfection of multiple Cas9 RNPs and donor DNAs.
source: Advantages of this approach include no detectable off-target editing, timed introduction of pre-assembled editing complexes into cells and simultaneous transfection of multiple Cas9 RNPs and donor DNAs.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach used.

claim: Cas9 RNP-mediated editing begins within 4 hr of delivery and is largely completed within 24 hr due to RNP degradation.
source: In addition, Cas9 RNP-mediated editing begins within 4 hr of delivery and is largely completed within 24 hr due to RNP degradation (Kim et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Higher cell viability has been observed following RNP transfection compared with DNA transfection.
source: Furthermore, higher cell viability has been observed following RNP transfection compared with DNA transfection (Kim et al., 2014; Zuris et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The system maximized the efficiency of HDR such that ∼33% of detected DSB repair events occur with homologous recombination of donor DNA.
source: Using this system, we have maximized the efficiency of HDR such that ∼33% of detected DSB repair events occur with homologous recombination of donor DNA.
evidence: This is supported by deep sequencing data showing the HDR/TE ratio.

claim: 10% HDR efficiency was reported in HEK293T cells at the EMX1 target using nucleic acid delivery.
source: We chose the EMX1 target sequence to compare with published results using nucleic acid delivery, for which 10% HDR efficiency was reported in HEK293T cells (Ran et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The results are significantly higher than reported rates of HDR in synchronized HCT116 cells using TALENs.
source: Our results are also significantly higher than reported rates of HDR in synchronized HCT116 cells using Transcription Activator-Like Effector Nucleases (TALENs) and higher than typically observed using nucleic acid-based delivery of Cas9 (Rivera-Torres et al., 2014). (Hsu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison with cited previous work.
